cues.text: Welcome to Study Session 6 of MIT 8103, Advanced Database Systems.
The topic is Database Integration, Data Security and Data Privacy, and this first chapter gives you the big picture of all three.
Let's begin with database integration.
Database integration means combining or coordinating data across different sources, so that people and systems get useful, consistent access to it.
There are several ways to do this.
You might use ETL or ELT, which are approaches for extracting data, transforming it and loading it into a target.
You might use APIs, federated queries, replication, or change data capture.
You might use data virtualisation, or master-data management.
Each of these is a different way of making separate data sources work together.
Integration is not easy, and the challenges are worth learning by name.
First, schema mismatch: different sources structure the same information differently.
Second, duplicate entities: the same real-world person or thing appears more than once.
Third, inconsistent units: one source might record a value in one unit and another source in a different unit.
Fourth, different identifiers: each source may label the same entity with its own key.
Fifth, stale data: some copies fall out of date.
Sixth, transactional boundaries: a transaction that is safe inside one system may not be guaranteed across several.
And seventh, security policies, which may differ from one source to the next.
Here is an example that shows why this matters.
Suppose several systems share a patient ID.
That shared ID requires governance and reliable matching.
And be careful, because merging records incorrectly can be harmful.
If two different patients are merged into one record, someone's health information could be wrongly attributed to another person.
Now to security.
Security protects data and systems from unauthorised access, alteration or interruption.
Those three words line up with the CIA triad: confidentiality, integrity and availability.
Confidentiality means only authorised parties can see the data.
Integrity means the data isn't improperly altered.
Availability means the system and data remain accessible when needed.
Privacy is a different idea.
Privacy concerns appropriate collection, use, disclosure and retention of personal data, along with the rights individuals have over that data.
Notice how that goes beyond protection from outsiders.
Here's the key point: a perfectly encrypted database can still violate privacy if it collects excessive data or uses it unlawfully.
The encryption may be flawless, yet the organisation may have collected too much, or used the data in ways it shouldn't.
So remember: privacy is broader than confidentiality.
Next, what counts as personal data?
Personal data is data that identifies, or relates to, an identifiable individual, either directly or indirectly.
Sensitive personal data includes categories such as health and biometric data under applicable law.
Notice the qualification: what counts as sensitive depends on the law that applies.
There is one more subtle point.
An identifier can remain personal even when names are removed, if linkage or reidentification is possible.
In other words, taking away the name does not automatically make the data anonymous.
If someone can link the remaining details back to a person, it is still personal data.
Finally, the privacy principles.
They are: lawfulness, fairness and transparency; purpose limitation; data minimisation; accuracy; storage limitation; and security and accountability.
In practice, this means you collect only what is necessary for the stated purposes.
You keep records accurate.
And you delete, or appropriately anonymise, data when retaining it is no longer justified.
Two design ideas tie these together.
Privacy by design means building these controls into the architecture of the system from the start.
Privacy by default means configuring the system so that exposure is the least necessary, without requiring the user to opt out.
The user shouldn't have to go and switch protections on; the protective setting is already the starting point.
